actions.justification: Mandatory first step - patient presents with worsening dyspnea and increased sputum, consistent with AECOPD. Respiratory status assessment (work of breathing, breath sounds, accessory muscle use) is critical to determine severity.
Mandatory - comprehensive vital sign assessment is required to establish baseline and detect hemodynamic instability or respiratory failure in this COPD/cor pulmonale patient.
Mandatory - chest X-ray is required to identify triggers of AECOPD (pneumonia, pneumothorax, pulmonary edema) and assess for complications in a patient with cor pulmonale.

MANDATORY: ABG is essential in AECOPD to assess for hypercapnic respiratory failure (elevated PaCO2), acidosis, and to guide oxygen therapy targets and NIV eligibility decisions. This must be completed within the 60-minute deadline.
In COPD with possible CO2 retention, altered mental status (confusion, drowsiness) is a critical sign of hypercapnic encephalopathy and would urgently change management toward NIV or intubation.

Given COPD and cor pulmonale, early assessment of NIV eligibility is recommended per AECOPD guidelines, especially if ABG reveals hypercapnic acidosis. Proactive eligibility assessment ensures readiness for rapid NIV initiation if needed.

Patient with COPD presenting with worsening dyspnea and increased sputum production suggests possible infectious exacerbation (AECOPD). Blood cultures should be obtained before initiating antibiotics to identify causative organisms.
COPD exacerbation guidelines recommend short-acting bronchodilators (e.g., salbutamol/ipratropium) as first-line treatment to relieve bronchospasm and improve airflow in acute exacerbations.
Supplemental oxygen is indicated for COPD exacerbation, targeting SpO2 88-92% to avoid hypercapnic respiratory failure given the patient's COPD and cor pulmonale comorbidities.
CBC to evaluate for leukocytosis suggesting infectious exacerbation, anemia contributing to dyspnea, or polycythemia common in COPD/cor pulmonale patients.
BMP to assess electrolytes, renal function, and bicarbonate (compensatory metabolic alkalosis in chronic hypercapnia), and to guide potential diuretic use in cor pulmonale.

Patient has COPD with cor pulmonale presenting with worsening dyspnea and increased sputum — pulmonology consultation appropriate for specialized management guidance including NIV decisions and exacerbation treatment optimization.
Procalcitonin helps differentiate bacterial from viral exacerbation in COPD, guiding antibiotic therapy decision. This is relevant given worsening dyspnea and increased sputum production.
Sputum culture should be obtained before initiating antibiotics to identify causative organism and guide targeted therapy in this COPD exacerbation with increased sputum.
Lactate helps assess for early tissue hypoperfusion or occult sepsis, which may complicate COPD exacerbation with infectious etiology.

Systemic corticosteroids (e.g., methylprednisolone or prednisone) are a cornerstone of AECOPD management, reducing treatment failure, length of stay, and relapse. Patient has COPD exacerbation with worsening dyspnea and increased sputum. GOLD guidelines recommend 40mg prednisolone for 5 days.

Antibiotics are indicated in AECOPD with increased sputum production (Anthonisen criteria). Blood and sputum cultures have already been ordered, so antibiotics can now be initiated. Appropriate antibiotic coverage (e.g., amoxicillin-clavulanate or azithromycin) per local protocols is recommended.

CT chest can help evaluate for complications such as pneumonia, pulmonary embolism (which can mimic or complicate AECOPD), or other structural changes relevant to this patient with cor pulmonale. Chest X-ray has already been ordered but CT provides more detailed assessment.

Patient has cor pulmonale which is associated with right heart failure and fluid retention. With worsening dyspnea, a diuretic is appropriate to reduce fluid overload. IV fluids would be contraindicated given cor pulmonale, and vasopressors are not needed with stable hemodynamics.

Patient with COPD and cor pulmonale presenting with worsening dyspnea. IV fluids may support perfusion given stable vitals, though should be used cautiously given cor pulmonale. This is one of the only available actions remaining in this phase. Administer conservatively while monitoring for fluid overload.

While MAP is currently adequate at 103 mmHg, vasopressor availability should be noted for cor pulmonale patients who may decompensate. This is among the remaining available actions in the current phase and can be held ready or used if hemodynamic status changes.
Patient has cor pulmonale; diuretics were given. Monitoring fluid balance and urine output is essential to assess diuretic response and prevent fluid overload or under-resuscitation.
Continuous SpO2 monitoring is essential in COPD with cor pulmonale to ensure adequate oxygenation without suppressing hypoxic drive, targeting SpO2 88-92%.

CBC, blood culture, ABG, sputum culture, BMP, lactate, and procalcitonin are all pending — reviewing results as they return will guide further management decisions including antibiotic selection and ventilatory support needs.
